utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please call the case, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Today, I'd like to greet, first and foremost, the accused, then the counsel, everybody from the OTP, and all those assisting us. I'd also like to greet a new face in the public gallery which will be of assistance during our session. We will continue with the closing argument of General Petkovic. According to the new calculation made by the Registrar, they have one hour and forty minutes left. So we gave you an extra five minutes, compared to what I told you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to our learned friends from the OTP, the accused, and my colleagues from the Defences, as well as to all those who are with us today. Yesterday, analysing the final brief of the OTP, we stopped at paragraph 22. At the very end of the paragraph, you can see there an assertion made by the OTP that Petkovic issued an order to arrest and isolate all able-bodied Muslims throughout HVO-controlled territory. Although we have discussed it to some extent, we can have another look at the right-hand side column, where you see the order issued by General Petkovic. I apologise. I forgot to say that we should go into Sanction. I hope we can resume. Apologies for omitting that in the first place. In the right-hand-side column, we see the order by General Petkovic, dated 30th June 1993. It is quite clear that it does not encompass the entire HVO-controlled territory, because it was issued to only one operational zone, which is South-Eastern Herzegovina. The commander of that operational zone forwarded the order to only two brigades, the 2nd and 3rd. Therefore, the assertion made by the Prosecution is incorrect. The next example is paragraph 28, in which the Prosecutor asserts that Praljak was present at the meeting on the 11th of May, 1993, and that the meeting was also attended by Petkovic and some others. I won't go into the specific names on this occasion. In the right-hand-side column, you see an excerpt from General Praljak's testimony, page 40761. You will see there that General Praljak did not say that the meeting was attended by General Petkovic. If we recall other evidence, we see that General Petkovic, on the 10th of May, 1993, in the evening, left for Kiseljak in order to meet with Sefer Halilovic. On the 11th of May, both of them, Sefer Halilovic and General Petkovic, arrived in Medjugorje. On the 12th of May, Halilovic and Petkovic signed an agreement on the cessation of hostilities. Therefore, the Prosecutor erroneously asserts that at the meeting referred to by General Praljak, General Petkovic was in attendance as well. The next example has to do with paragraph 104, which is legal in nature. However, I found it necessary to refer to it briefly. In this paragraph, the Prosecutor mentions the crime of terrorising civilians, which can be committed with a direct or indirect intention. In the right-hand-side column, although this is a legal matter, we prepared for you an excerpt from the appeals judgement in the Galic case, paragraph 104; as well as the appeal judgement in the Milosevic case, paragraph 37; and the first-instance judgement in the Galic case, paragraph 136, with the accompanying footnote, which clearly indicates that the crime of terrorising civilians can only be committed with a special, specific intention or intent. The following paragraph we wanted to draw your attention to is paragraph 193 of the final brief of the OTP. The Prosecutor asserts that Petkovic, having testified about Operation South, wanted to paint a wrong picture before the Chamber about the true nature of that operation. We wanted to direct your attention at the following: The Prosecutor, during their case, did not state a single word about Operation South, although they had conducted an interview with the commander of that operation. Therefore, they had all necessary knowledge about the purpose and intent of that operation. The Petkovic Defence was the only one to include that operation in our case, because the events which occurred during the operation were of paramount importance for the withdrawal of Petkovic from the position of the chief of the Main Staff. Therefore, it is completely unfounded to state that the Petkovic Defence wanted to do anything before the Trial Chamber concerning Operation South in order to try to paint an erroneous picture. The next issue has to do with paragraph 648, in which the Prosecutor asserts in the chief of the Main Staff, I quote: "... was superior to the HVO Command Staff." Given that the Prosecution, in their opening statement objected to the way the Petkovic Defence interpreted certain legal provisions, we need to look at the wording of the provision, itself, in the right-hand-side column and to see what it was that the OTP omitted when describing the position of the chief of the Main Staff. The Prosecution omitted the following: that the chief of the Main Staff is superior to the HVO Command within the scope of general and specific powers vested in him by the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Your Honours, this is not the sole example of the Prosecution interpreting certain legal provisions by quoting only parts of those provisions, thus displaying an incorrect interpretation of the entire legislation. Had they quoted the entire sentence, they would had to have admitted that the chief of the Main Staff was not superior to all military commanders in all matters, because it would go against their case against General Petkovic. In this context, at page 277 of their brief, the OTP state that Petkovic was at all relevant times either the number one or number two HVO military commander. We reiterate, Your Honours, as we also said in our final brief, that Petkovic was the chief of the Main Staff, and that rights, duties and obligations of the chief of the Main Staff, as the chief of any other staff, are not identical to the rights and obligations of a commander. Given that we have discussed this issue at length in our final brief, we do not find it necessary to repeat all of our theses at this point. In paragraph 162 of the final brief, the Prosecution states that Petkovic could not recall who he received his salary from. We discussed this at length during re-examination of General Petkovic, and we'll try to sum up everything that took place in that regard. The Prosecution referred to Petkovic's testimony in the Kordic case. We prepared parts of the transcript in the following few pages, and it is clearly stated there that Petkovic had no problem whatsoever recalling who he received his salary from. However, in the Kordic case, he was limited, in terms of questions and answers. Those limitations were set by the Republic of Croatia, which also had its representatives in the proceedings. That limitation also referred to the issue of salary whilst serving with the HVO. There were no such limitations in this case. Therefore, it is unambiguous, as it was also clearly stated by General Petkovic that while serving with the HVO, he received his salary from the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. Therefore, in the final brief, the Prosecution completely erroneously commented upon Petkovic's testimony, in our view attempting to contaminate the entire testimony and show it to be -- not to be credible. We'll skip over a few pages. The next example has to do with paragraph 881, in which the Prosecution asserts the following, I quote: [In English] "... as Pringle so amply stated, behaviour like Petkovic ..." [Interpretation] End of quote. When I read this part of the final brief of the Prosecution, I indeed thought that Andrew Pringle did comment on Petkovic's behaviour. Being unable to recall it, I went back to Andrew Pringle's report. In the footnote, we see that it is paragraph 68. We are going to show you paragraph 68 in the right-hand-side column. In that paragraph, there is no reference to General Petkovic the way the OTP stated. Therefore, the Prosecution erroneously presented the contents of paragraph 68 to the Chamber, thus contaminating the evidence and rendering separate meaning to it which the evidence does not possess. The next example is paragraph 882, which has to do with Prozor in October 1992. Here, it is stated that Petkovic was familiar with en masse forcible transfers of Muslims, as well as deportations. With regard to this example about Prozor, we wanted to draw your attention to the following fact: The OTP never charged any of the accused for the crime of deportation in Prozor in October 1992. They did not do anything of the sort concerning forcible transfer that allegedly was committed in October 1992 in Prozor. Therefore, the crimes which should make part of the Prosecution case with respect to JCE 1 do not form part of it, and the Prosecution did not put forth any charges regarding that issue. The next example is paragraph 883 pertaining to the same type of crime. It has to do with Gornji Vakuf. We have discussed this at some length in our final brief because we were limited by the word count. I can sum it up as follows: None of the accused were accused of deportation in Gornji Vakuf in 1992. An analysis conducted by the Petkovic Defence indicates that the Prosecutor did not prove that the civilians were forcibly transferred from Prozor in January and February 1993. The next example has to do with paragraph 885 of the final brief. The Prosecution refers to a letter of the 23rd of April, 1993. Apparently, it was sent by Petkovic to Mate Boban. The letter itself had to do with certain crimes committed in Central Bosnia, as reported to General Petkovic by Tihomir Blaskic. In the right-hand-side column, you see the beginning of the letter. We indicated this excerpt in order to show that, indeed, it concerns Central Bosnia. What we wanted to say is the following: The crimes committed in Central Bosnia in April 1993 do not form the crime base of this case. We also believe that this document is important because it unambiguously indicates that unlawful activities described in the letter were not something that had been planned or wished for by HVO commanders. Had it been the case, they would not have reported about it to their superiors. The next example is paragraph 887. The Prosecutor asserts that the Monitors of the European Commission and other international representatives condemned Petkovic and his behaviour. The Prosecutor does not specify a single footnote or piece of evidence to corroborate this. What we wish to say about it is the following: According to our analysis of all UNPROFOR documents, as well as ECMM documents and the documents of other international representatives, Petkovic was never seen or portrayed as an extremist; rather, he was shown to be a moderate person who was always in favour of an agreement. As regards the hawk-dove system, if we take into account that simple division, Petkovic was always seen as a dove. The next example which we'll dwell on has to do with paragraph 953 of the final brief, as well as paragraph 825 and 826 and 831, as well as parts of the closing arguments of Ms. West at page 52054 of the transcript. All these examples have to do with the alleged role Petkovic played in the destruction of Stari Most, the Old Bridge. The entire thesis of the Prosecution relies or hinges on a single document, which is P6534, which is an order of the 8th November 1993. In the right-hand-side column, Your Honours, you see excerpts of that order prepared in the Croatian language so that you could see that the order does not contain a signature. Therefore, the document does not have the signature of General Petkovic. This fact alone need not mean much, but let us take a closer look. I would like to remind you that this is 8 November 1993. General Praljak, on transcript pages 41270, speaking about document 4D834, said that General Petkovic had not been at Citluk on 8 November 1993, and that is why one order or one invitation was signed by Slobodan Praljak, although it bears the name "Milivoj Petkovic," so that Praljak gave evidence that on 8 November, General Petkovic was not at Citluk. Milivoj Petkovic, on transcript pages 49643, confirmed that, indeed, on that day he was not at Citluk, but in Split, because on 7 November he was to meet General Briquemont. Let us look at document 4D2026, which is General Petkovic's document. He sent it to the UNPROFOR Command at Kiseljak. I repeat the number, 4D2026. General Petkovic confirms having met General Briquemont on 7 November at Divulje, which is just outside Split, so that, Your Honours, the evidence confirms that Petkovic, on 8 November 1993, was not at Citluk and did not sign the order issued on that day about artillery activity. What we consider very important is the fact that all this evidence we have just cited was known to the Prosecution, because we've seen it in this courtroom several times, but the Prosecution intentionally neglected this evidence to draw General Petkovic into their story as the person responsible for the destruction of the Old Bridge in Mostar, as it were. We invite you, Your Honours, to assess all this evidence and conclude what the truth is. The next example is paragraph 872. It's about the meeting between General Petkovic and Ratko Mladic in early July 1993. In this section of Ratko Mladic's diaries, the alleged words of Petkovic are related: "Push your cannons forward a bit and let my guys from Travnik die. They haven't fought, anyway." In responding to submission that this excerpt from the diary be admitted into evidence, we objected based on the fact that this doesn't make sense. There is no logic in Petkovic firing at HVO soldiers. And apart from that, Travnik fell a month earlier, and at Travnik there were no HVO soldiers at all. I needn't go into this document any deeper, but we are really impressed by the quality of faith the Prosecution put into Mladic's diary. If Mladic should stand trial before this Tribunal one day, we are curious to -- we will be curious to see how much Mladic's diaries will be trusted. The next example is from paragraph 900. The Prosecution claim that Petkovic's statement that he never received Ivica Rajic's report of 23 October 1993 is not credible, and they say: "This Petkovic evasion again holds no water." Your Honours, in our final brief, we discuss the topic of Stupni Do at length because we consider it very relevant, and we think that this case is directly linked with General Petkovic's responsibility. That's why we plan to deal with this matter for a couple of minutes. On the right-hand side, we see the Croatian report of Ivica Rajic. It is shown in Croatian to enable you to see that this report, Ivica Rajic's report, contains an instruction for General Petkovic from General Praljak to take care of the situation in Vares. We are showing this document because it is addressed to Milivoj Petkovic at the Main Staff, and we can see that the document indeed made it to the Main Staff, which is confirmed by the handwritten words of General Praljak. If we read this document in Croatian, then this document proves that a document which was supposed to reach Milivoj Petkovic at the Main Staff indeed arrived at the Main Staff. The Prosecution showed us no evidence that shows that this document was indeed forwarded from the Main Staff to Petkovic in Kiseljak. The next example refers to paragraph 933. The Prosecution asserts that Petkovic repeatedly received information from his soldiers about the harassment and mistreatment of prisoners and detainees along the front-line. In the footnote, there's a reference to document P6202. In the right column, there is the document, itself. This is a document which, on the 28th of October, 1993, was sent by Stanko Bozic, the number-one man at Heliodrom, to Milivoj Petkovic. Our conclusions are the following: One, the allegation is completely false that commanders informed Petkovic about anything concerning the prisoners and their labour on the front-line. And, secondly, this document contains not a single word about mistreatment or labour on the front-line: This report of Bozic's is the only report he sent to Petkovic, and we have clearly pointed that out in Annex 12 to our final brief. In paragraph 937, the Prosecution asserts that Petkovic had information about the wounding and deaths of prisoners forced to work, and that he received information about that repeatedly from the representatives of the international community. The Prosecution also asserts that Petkovic had that information while he was issuing orders concerning forcible labour. In the footnotes, documents P5308 and P5967 are referred to. In the right column, you can see the dates of these documents. One is from late September, and the other from October 1993. Our conclusions are the following: The Prosecution failed to prove that Petkovic had information about killed and wounded detainees in July and August 1993, when he issued three orders in relation to the labour of the detainees and prisoners. Thus, Petkovic spoke the truth, because he spoke about his knowledge at the moment he issued these orders and not later. The next example is about paragraph 962. Here, the Prosecution refers to the topic of shelling and sniping, and they say that Petkovic had information about that. The date of 23 September 1993 is mentioned as the day when Pasalic complained to UNPROFOR. About this, we wish to conclude that this shows that before September 1993, there were no complaints about shelling by the HVO or about sniping of HVO members. The following example is paragraph 964, in which the Prosecution asserts that Petkovic personally denied humanitarian convoys free passage. About this paragraph, we -- or rather there were several footnotes to this paragraph which you see on the left, and on the right you can see the list of documents with the dates of issuance. We have no time now, Your Honours, but I believe there is even no need to go into each and every of these documents, but we wish to draw your attention to two documents which are extremely important to our minds. The first such document is P3923. It's a letter sent by Tadic to Jadranko Prlic on 3 August 1993, in which Darinko Tadic complaints that he didn't get an approval from General Petkovic for the passage of a convoy from Bosnia to Split and back. So this is a letter dated 3 August 1993. Let's take a look at the following document, P3895. This is an order by General Petkovic issued one day earlier on 2 August 1993 and sent to all HVO units. It is said here very clearly and unambiguously that pursuant to the Makarska Agreement, as well as the Sarajevo Airport Agreement, all HVO units shall enable the unobstructed passage of convoys of humanitarian aid. Therefore, there is no evidence showing that General Petkovic obstructed the passage of any convoy carrying humanitarian aid. The following example is about the chapter in the Prosecution final brief in which it is asserted that Petkovic had at his disposal various means to discipline HVO members, and in Annex G there is also an overview of documents about the possibility of disciplining, which partly relates to General Petkovic. Your Honours, we invite you to scrutinise these documents from Annex G very carefully, because we will all easily establish that the Prosecution failed to mention a single law or regulation which would enable Petkovic to punish or exert control as asserted by the Prosecution. And, furthermore, the following clearly follows from Annex G: If Petkovic really knew the name of the perpetrator and the crime committed, then certain measures were taken. If, however, the perpetrator was unidentified, Petkovic issued general instructions that appropriate investigative measures and sanctions shall be taken. In that context, my learned friend Mr. Scott, on transcript pages 51935 and the following, referred to document P1598, which you can see in the right column. It is obvious from this document that General Petkovic issued an order that an investigation shall be launched against a member of the Main Staff, an officer in the Main Staff of the HVO, concerning the misuse of a stamp. We would like to stress that this is about a person who worked in the Main Staff; that is, a person who was immediately subordinate to General Petkovic. He knew about this misconduct and immediately took measures he considered appropriate, but the Prosecution shows no evidence that any other officer or any other employee in the Main Staff committed a crime against a Muslim about which Petkovic knew but failed to do anything about it. The following examples from paragraph 876, 930, 931, and 957, and 962 refer to an interesting standard for mens rea systematically used by the Prosecution in their final brief not only with regard to General Petkovic but also the other accused. For example, I quote: "It is impossible that Petkovic was not aware ..." Or: "Petkovic could not have been aware ..." Or: "He would have had to try very hard not to be aware of it." Your Honours, I think we all agree that these are not legal standards for mens rea, as recognised by this Tribunal, and we really fail to understand what the Prosecution really want to achieve with such language when it comes to the mens rea of the accused. The next paragraph is 973. This is a very important paragraph for General Petkovic. Here, the Prosecution asserts that Petkovic, among other things, ordered murder, as charged in Counts 2 and 3, and they go on to explain in the footnote -- that is, in paragraph 1308, that these orders were about prisoners of war who were killed during forcible labour, forced labour. With regard to this, we wish to say the following: Firstly, the Prosecution failed to prove that based on Milivoj Petkovic's order, the crime of forced labour of prisoners of war was committed. In addition, the Prosecutor failed to prove that pursuant to any of Milivoj Petkovic's orders about forced labour, any detainee was killed. Therefore, Milivoj Petkovic can certainly not be held responsible for the alleged orders to kill prisoners of war during forced labour. The same topic was discussed by my learned friend Ms. West, and she said that, one, Petkovic's order, dated 8 August 1993, was executed, or, rather, that pursuant to that order, a crime was committed, and the crime was forced labour by prisoners of war. Let's look at the right-hand side of the page. First of all, the order number is 4020, dated 8 August 1993. We see that it was sent to the Posusje Brigade, and everybody else was copied. Let's look at the content of the order. The first sentence reads: "Order to fortify the achieved lines immediately." That's the first sentence in the order, and that's an order, of course. The second sentence reads: "Prisoners and detained Muslims may be used for fortifying lines." The second sentence is a permission to use prisoners and detained Muslims. And then the third sentence reads, and it is an instruction: "To file a request to use prisoners." An elementary school investigative analysis of this order, in our view, Your Honours, show that this is not an order for prisoners of war to be used for forced labour. However, it is a permission to use prisoners of war, amongst others, who are sent to work. Let's see what happened next. Document P4030, this is a request issued by the Posusje Brigade Command. He is requesting to use detainees. I would like to emphasise that a reference here is made to Muslim detainees who will be performing certain tasks. And the following document is P4068, 4068. Your Honours, the document is presented here in both versions, in Croatian and English. We would like to draw your attention to an error in translation. It is very clear in the Croatian text that a hundred detainees were taken over, detainees; whereas in the English translation, a reference is made to a hundred prisoners. If this document had been translated properly, it would arise from it that a hundred detainees had been taken over, and not a hundred prisoners of war. And the following fact is also important in the analysis of this document: There is no single piece of evidence about the type of work that these hundred individuals were engaged in, irrespective of their status, whether they were detainees or prisoners of war. It is also important to say that there is no single piece of evidence proving that those people worked voluntarily or that they had been forced to perform those tasks. In other words, were they volunteers or were they forced to do labour? Why do we mention voluntary labour? Because of a witness who was detained in the prison in Vitina. The witness was protected, so the documents should not be broadcast. Let's look at P10210. On page 3, Witness EI said, inter alia, and I quote: [In English] "Every morning, one of the guards would come to the hangar and look for volunteers to go work for them. Some prisoners volunteered as they were promised better food and also as the hangar was made from tin, the temperature was sometimes 40 degrees inside, so it was better to be outside even if it was to work." [Interpretation] The witness also testified about work which could not be considered inadmissible, and he also mentioned the types of work which could be considered inadmissible. In this context, Your Honours, we would like to point to the practice of this Tribunal, which we believe is best illustrated by the first-instance judgement in the Naletilic case, paragraph 259. In that paragraph, it is stated, and I quote: [In English] "As a result of the foregoing, the Chamber will have to determine, on a case-by-case basis, whether the forms of labour alleged in the indictment were indeed undertaken voluntarily or whether the detainees were compelled to do so." [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are familiar with the practice of this Tribunal, and we know that some circumstances make voluntary labour look different because of the circumstances. However, there is an undisputed fact that the Trial Chamber has to take all of the circumstances of each case into account. In this case, we have not dealt with that. Let's conclude about all that has been said so far. Petkovic's order was not an order for the unlawful labour of prisoners of war. It is, however, permission that certain work could be done by using prisoners and detainees. There is no evidence that any prisoner of war had to do any unlawful labour. There's also no evidence that detainees were forced to work. With regard to the topic of unlawful labour, there are two other Petkovic's orders. Since the Prosecution agrees with the Petkovic Defence that nothing was done in order to execute those two orders, we are not going to waste any time on them. I would just like to draw your attention to our final brief, where the topic was covered at great length. And now we come to the topic of the siege of Mostar. Maybe some day Ms. West and I will co-author a paper on the topic because we spent so much time discussing it. On transcript page 52069, my learned friend Ms. West said, in a nutshell, that Muslim civilians could not leave East Mostar. Your Honours, we don't have any more time, nor do we think that it is necessary to deal with main routes and alternative routes that led from East Mostar towards Jablanica and further on towards Central Bosnia. However, in this case there is no dispute about the following thing: First of all, there's no single piece of evidence that any of the civilians was killed or wounded while leaving East Mostar and going towards Jablanica. There is no single piece of evidence showing that the HVO opened either artillery or any type of fire to prevent any individual or group of civilians who wanted to leave East Mostar and go in the direction of Jablanica. As we look at the evidence on file, we can see that there is no proof that anybody was either killed or wounded. The most important thing for this topic is the issue whether that communication was at all possible and whether that communication was en masse. As we go on, we will be using exclusively Prosecutor's evidence to show that the communication was indeed possible, that the communication was en masse, and that the communication was basically hindered by the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The first document that we would like to show you is a protected document, and that's why I'm not going to talk about the contents. I'm just going to give you the number of the document, P9181. And this document, at the end of the chapter that we are showing to you, it says: [In English] "The movement remains limited due to the danger of the journey and the fact that BiH ..." "[Interpretation] I would like to repeat the number, P9851, 9851. I'm not going to repeat the entire sentence. I'll continue: [In English] "... and the fact that the BiH Army permission must be obtained to leave, such permission reportedly being difficult to obtain." [Interpretation] The following evidence that we would like to draw your attention to is Witness BB's testimony, transcript page 25335. The witness said as follows, I quote: [In English] "We were very well aware of the --"

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now continuing on the same topic, let's look at 4D719. This is a report about the situation in the area north of East Mostar. We have seen the document a lot of times in this courtroom. Let's look at it once again. The 4th Command of the BiH Army controlled that area and established, I quote: "... a great problem for the command of the operational group is transport of civilian population and others marching in the direction of north and south. That is why it is necessary for civil authorities to take over the transport of civilians. There are huge problems with the transport of wounded people and other things required by the town. There is a need to repair the armoured transporter for this purpose and its usage in night-time." And just one more document about that topic. This is an excerpt from Esad Sejtanic's book. This is on page 184, and I quote -- I will just read the last sentence. You see the entire chapter: "By repressive measures, regrettably, we prevented the outflow of the population and reduced any movement of population to the minimum." I conclude, Your Honours, the Prosecutor's documents and documents issued by the BiH Army and its members fully confirm the fact that people could leave East Mostar en masse, that the population used the routes available to them, but the Muslim authorities -- or, rather, the BiH Army prevented the departure of civilians en masse. I am not talking about the lawfulness of such procedures on the part of the BiH Army, but I believe that it is very important in these proceedings to put the siege of Mostar in context. And now we are at the very end of our analysis of the Prosecutor's final brief. In paragraph 308 [as interpreted], the Prosecutor asks for a sentence of 40 years, and the Prosecutor bases that request on the following. The paragraph is 1308. Firstly, if we look at the speech, that was never uttered, and then he bases the request on the order of 30th June 1993 about the isolation of the Muslim soldiers of the HVO and military conscripts of the BiH Army who were also reserve force of the BiH Army, and, as we said -- and as we showed, the decision was legitimate and was issued for security reasons. A request for such a sentence, the Prosecutor bases on the assertion that Valentin Coric [as interpreted]ordered that POWs be used for forced labour, although there is not a single piece of evidence in existence to show that any POW performed any forced labour pursuant to Petkovic's order. Their request further relies on the assertion that Mr. Petkovic, having issued orders in July and August 1993, knew of the wounding and killing of people who had to do the labour, although documents confirm that, first, such knowledge was gained by Petkovic as late as September and October 1993 for the first time. Finally, their request is based on the assertion that Petkovic participated in an orchestrated cover-up of the crime in Stupni Do. The Prosecutor knows well that Petkovic, as deputy chief of the Main Staff or deputy commander of the Main Staff, had no commanding authority and could not independently take any action. He could only work according to orders and instructions of his superiors. As of 9 November 1993, Ante Roso was at the helm of the Main Staff. We did not put forth a single piece of evidence in this courtroom which would have to do with Ante Roso, the chief of the Main Staff, and his opinion or position vis-a-vis the crimes committed in Stupni Do. This is what we wanted to tell you about the Prosecution final brief, in its part which directly affects General Petkovic. We will now go back to General Petkovic, himself, wishing to show you what was the level of Petkovic's knowledge, his mens rea and actus reus in the relevant period of time. Let us look at document P279. I apologise for the mistake. We have the wrong year recorded. The document is actually from 1992. This is the speech that was not delivered, which the Prosecution stipulates as the only item which would connect Petkovic with anti-Muslim activities and the like. We once more wish to state that this speech was supposed to have been delivered, but was not, at the meeting with municipal representatives specified in paragraph 2. We also wanted to draw your attention to the fact that in this speech that was not delivered, it was recorded that still certain parts of the municipalities of Mostar and Stolac were not liberated because parts of those municipalities were at that point in time still under the control of the Serb forces. Therefore, the topic of liberation and introduction of Croatian rule in all municipalities referred to in the meeting was actually excluding the parts of Mostar and Stolac that had not been liberated. As for the interpretation of this speech that was never held, you can take our word for it or you can take the word of the Prosecution for it. However, we suggest that we view this document in the context of other documents by General Petkovic to see what the true meaning of the document is. The true meaning is also visible if we look at 4D830, which is also P907. That is Petkovic's report for the period of 1992. In its conclusions, it unambiguously states that HVO controls 90 per cent of the territory envisaged as the Croatian entity. HVO, therefore, has no need for any offensive operations, and it is stated that the HVO is fully capable to defend the liberated areas. Furthermore, it states that HVO controls 70 per cent of the free territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. A logical conclusion is that the remaining 30 per cent is controlled by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Therefore, it is beyond dispute that the free territory was seen to comprise both the territory held by the HVO and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Finally, the sentence that is of utmost importance is this: "The Croatian people, having organised their own armed forces, managed to defend not only themselves, but also the majority of Muslims." In our view, it unambiguously confirms that it was not the intention of either the HVO or the author of this report to undertake any anti-Muslim activities. The goal was to defend both Croats and Muslims, and that was the task of the HVO. It is also confirmed by the next few documents, which we'll only touch upon. Document 4D397, the 20th of June, 1992. Petkovic sent a letter to the HVO in Konjic and Gornji Vakuf. Inter alia, he says: "On behalf of Croats and Muslims, I beg you to overcome this situation. As the members of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you are bound to do that." The next example is P633, an order of the 23rd of October, 1992, to the HVO in Tomislavgrad. Petkovic states: "Find and talk to those with the greatest responsibility and influence." The next document is 4D399 of the 16th of November, 1992, an order to Zeljko Siljeg, commander of an operational zone. Petkovic states: "Get in touch urgently with the Command of the BH Army in Gornji Vakuf to overcome mistrust ..." The next document is 4D389, an order of the 16th of December, 1992, which Petkovic sent to Zeljko Siljeg and Tihomir Blaskic: "In executing this order, achieve full co-ordination with Bosnian Army units." The next document, P1115, January 13, 1993. Petkovic issued this order to the HVO in several municipalities. He states: "Where possible, set up joint teams with the Muslim side to solve the past or current conflicts." The next document, P1190, January 18, 1993, Petkovic's letter to the HVO in Central Bosnia. He states: "Please avoid conflicts of any kind, because we and the Muslims do not want our dispute to escalate again." Document 4D433 of January 20, 1993. Petkovic issued an order to the HVO in Konjic: "Establish contact with the BH Army in Konjic ..." The next document, 4D19, dated January 27, 1993. Petkovic states: "Resolve all disputes through negotiations ..." February 9, 1993, document 4D75, Petkovic's letter to Halilovic: "I looked forward to each new soldier, Croatian or Muslim, because I knew that they had a common goal." March 23, 1993, document P1709, a joint order by Petkovic and Pasalic: "Resolve all disagreements by joint agreements with mutual understanding and readiness by both sides to make concessions." April 18, 1993, Petkovic to all operational zones. It is document P1959. Petkovic states: "Establish communication with the BH Army Command ..." Mostar, May 9, 1993. Let us recall the testimony of General Petkovic at transcript page 49541, among others. As soon as Petkovic had learned of the conflict, he advised Mate Boban to get in touch with Alija Izetbegovic. He tried to contact Sefer Halilovic personally. We see the result of that the next day, May 10, 1993. Mate Boban and Alija Izetbegovic issue an order on a cease-fire. That is document 4D456 and 4D457. May 10, 1993, to May 12, 1993. Petkovic was with Sefer Halilovic throughout that period of time. Their meeting resulted in an agreement, which is P2344. June 1, 1993, document P2599, Petkovic's order to all operational zones: "... negotiate with the Muslim side ..." June 9, 1993, the fall of Travnik. Petkovic explains his reaction upon having learned of the fall. It is page 49456 of the transcript. Petkovic asked to meet Halilovic. The next document, 4D1355, General Petkovic's interview to the daily "Vecernji List" in August 1994. General Petkovic explains how he had come to Bosnia-Herzegovina with the intention of staying for about a month, but he remained longer. What is of importance to us is the following: General Petkovic, in 1994, said that the results of fighting the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were not very favourable for the HVO, but the reason was probably in that the HVO had not prepared for a war with the Muslim side. This is the truth, Your Honours. This is Petkovic's truth. It may not be an absolute, objective truth, but it is the truth of General Petkovic. We are coming to the end of General Petkovic's closing arguments. We pondered on what we should tell you by way of conclusion to indicate what was the most important thing for General Petkovic at the time. Therefore, we decided to show you a number of documents which would indicate that the HVO was a legal armed force and that it was a part of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as that all HVO fighters in Bosnia and Herzegovina as it exists today honours their service in the HVO, much as they do to all former members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This shows that the HVO was not a criminal armed force put together in order to implement a criminal enterprise. It fought for Bosnia-Herzegovina, much as the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina did. All rights that the fighters of the army are entitled to are also extended to HVO fighters. We showed you those documents in our Annex 1 of the final brief. Perhaps we can have another look at them. Document P2002, agreement between Halilovic and Petkovic. The date is April 20, 1993. In item 1, it is stated: "The B and H Army and the HVO are legitimate military forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and are accorded equal treatment." Document P2078 of April 24, 1993, a joint statement by Izetbegovic, Boban and Tudjman. Inter alia, mention is made on the agreement on the legal status of both the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO. The next document is P2091, annex to the aforementioned joint statement signed by Halilovic and Petkovic. It is stated: "The Army of B and H and the HVO will keep their individual identities and establishment of the command." "They will form the joint command ...," in item 2. Document 4D1234, the Washington Agreement, in which both sides are mentioned which were to establish a joint military command, that is to say, the HVO and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Document 4D826, Law on Armed Forces of the BH Federation, dated 1996. It is stated that: "The Army of the Federation is composed of the formations of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Council ..." Your Honours, have a look at the second paragraph of this document. In this document from 1996, it is stated: [In English] "Peacetime forces are constituted of (civilian) persons in the service of the Federation, conscripts and professional troops." [Interpretation] We wish to draw your attention to the language "conscripts," the word "conscripts." As we have extensively argued, we consider this to be a crucial notion in this trial. As shown in this document in 1996, conscripts of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were considered members of the armed forces. The following document is 2D628, the Law on the Rights of Defenders and Members of their Families from 2004. It shows that the same rights are enjoyed by members of the BH Army and HVO members. Document 2D1183 is the Law on the Special Rights of Recipients of War Decorations from 2005. We can see that extends to both members of the BH Army and members of the Croatian Defence Council. And the last document we're about to show is 2D1181, a decree on old-age pensions under favourable conditions from 2007. We see that it applies both to members of the BH Army and members of the HVO in the same way. Your Honours, we will finish by the break. We only have a few final remarks. Milivoj Petkovic and his Defence have never claimed that he is infallible, neither as a man nor as a professional soldier. Maybe today, based on all the information we have today, Milivoj Petkovic would have taken some other decisions in his life and in his military career. It is certain, however, that Petkovic came to Bosnia-Herzegovina in good faith to defend, as a professional soldier, first and foremost, his homeland, Croatia, which was attacked -- being attacked from the territory of BiH, but also to help the Croatian and Muslim peoples to defend themselves in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He participated in the creation and development of the Croatian Defence Council, as an army of both the Croatian and the Muslim peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Petkovic honestly believed that the Croatian Defence Council was one of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. All BH legislation confirmed that today -- confirms that today. Neither Milivoj Petkovic nor his colleagues planned to wage war on the BH Army, nor did they prepare for that war. Maybe that is why the BH Army was so successful in taking territory controlled by the Herceg-Bosna authorities from April 1993 on. Your Honours, we saw from numerous documents that Petkovic was not a man of war. Remember his words from the clip that we showed to you in our opening statement, Your Honours. I quote: "It is better to talk for two years than to wage war for one day." This is Milivoj Petkovic. General Petkovic gave testimony before you, Your Honours. It wasn't easy for him. It takes strength to do that. General Petkovic wanted to show you that all his acts were guided by military logic and that were justified from the military point of view. They may not have been the best, but surely they weren't criminal and most certainly not directed against the civilian Muslim population. We invite you, Your Honours, to assess the facts based on a comprehensive analysis of all evidence and the correct determination of the context of Petkovic's actions or omissions. We especially invite you to establish precisely what the legal obligations of the chief of the Main Staff of the HVO were under the legislation of Herceg-Bosna pursuant to the decisions of the supreme commander. Milivoj Petkovic was chief of Main Staff, and his position must not be confused with the position of a military commander. We believe, Your Honours, that in that case, you will find out that Milivoj Petkovic hasn't committed any one crime, that the Prosecution failed to prove that he ordered or instigated or aided or abetted anybody in the commission of crimes or that he was -- or that he is in any other way criminally responsible for crimes committed. An acquitting verdict will then be the only correct decision. This is the end of the Petkovic Defence final arguments. I wish to thank you, Your Honours, for the good co-operation during these five years. I would also like to thank my learned friends from the Prosecution, who showed much understanding for our applications to be awarded additional time. And we also considered that the Prosecution must be given a chance to do a good job, because if they do, that will place the Petkovic Defence in a favourable position as well. I would like to thank our colleagues from the other Defences for their co-operation. I would like to thank the Registry and all persons who assisted us, and especially to the interpreters, with special emphasis on the French booth. Thank you.

Your Honour, I know it's about time for the break, but at some point today, and I just want to alert the Chamber or raise it with the Chamber at the least inconvenient moment and without obstructing the Coric closing that will begin in a few minutes, I can only assume -- Mr. Stringer and I and the Prosecution team can only assume at some point the Chamber will want to hear thoughts in terms of connection -- requests for rebuttal before we actually get up against that time, so that everyone, including, of course, most importantly the Chamber, can plan accordingly. Based on what the Prosecution has heard so far, we do expect to request a substantial amount of rebuttal. I don't know when the Chamber will want to take that up. We're prepared to address it today, but we just raise it and put it in the Chamber's hands so that that can be addressed at the appropriate moment, but presumably not -- not at the last minute, so to speak. Thank you.

The Bench thinks that we are yet to hear the closing arguments of the Coric Defence and the Pusic Defence, and, therefore, it is only after that we will move on to that stage of the trial when it's the Prosecution's turn for their response. Then we will deal with your position, and not at this moment, while we will entertain only the closing argument of the Defences. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We continue with the trial. I give the floor to the Coric Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. At the beginning of the closing arguments on behalf of the Valentin Coric team, I would like to extend my thanks to everybody who, with their committed efforts, have contributed to our bringing this trial to an end, to the Judges, and all employees of the Chamber, my learned friends from the Prosecution, and all Prosecution staff, my colleagues from the Defence and all members of their teams, the Registry, the technical personnel, the security guards, and especially our interpreters deserve all our thanks, because without them, our voice would remain unheard. I would like to use this opportunity to thank all those who I may have forgotten to mention. After several years of trial and after analysing the statements of hundreds of witnesses contained in over 50.000 pages of the transcripts and over 10.000 documents, two weeks ago we were able to hear the Prosecution's final and best arguments. We listened to the Prosecution closing arguments patiently. For all of us who have seen all evidence in this trial and heard all witnesses, both the Prosecution as well as Defence witnesses, it was difficult to listen to the Prosecution closing arguments patiently. It was just as difficult as it was to read the Prosecution final brief. It was difficult, Your Honours, because both the Prosecution final brief and their closing arguments were intended to divert the attention of the Trial Chamber from the evidence led, but instead wanted to focus the attention of the Trial Chamber to insinuations instead of concrete facts. Your Honours, at the end of their closing arguments, the Prosecution mentioned the victims of various conflicts throughout human history, including the victims of the Holocaust. Every victim, even if it's one single person, deserves justice. And the Valentin Coric Defence deeply and honestly sympathises with each victim, but not one of the victims mentioned, not even the victims of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, cannot be compared with the Holocaust for one important reason. Terrible as their fate may have been, and as much as we all may sympathise with them, all these victims were members of warring parties, whereas the victims of the Holocaust were not. They were systematically exterminated only because they were Jews. After the closing arguments of the Prosecution, I was thinking how I should start my closing arguments, and then something occurred to me that I had heard some time ago from a more experienced and wiser colleague. She said to me, When a common man reads the contents of an indictment in the media, for that common man, the accused is already guilty, he is as good as convicted. Talking about the judgement of the public, there is no principle that nobody is guilty until his guilt is proved beyond reasonable doubt. Why am I saying that? Because during the closing arguments of the Prosecution, we heard the indictment once more. But, Your Honours, we are -- we do not stand trial before the public or a lay jury. These accused are being tried by professional Judges who, based on the analysis of all evidence, will individually and, together with all other Judges, will decide whether this Prosecution was able to prove the allegations in the indictment beyond reasonable doubt. At the end of his closing arguments, my learned friend Mr. Scott, in the manner of a true knight of international justice, appealed to the Court to listen to the voices of the victims. Your Honours, international justice includes satisfaction for the victims, but not in line with the Machiavelli's principle of achieving your goal at any cost. International justice was -- protecting the rights of the victims, includes establishing the truth and protecting the rights of the accused. International justice means that this Prosecution must prove the defendant Valentin Coric guilty beyond reasonable doubt. The Prosecution wishes to present itself as knights of international justice. With all due respect for my learned friends from the Prosecution, Your Honours, in the case of Valentin Coric, this Prosecution has not acted in the least knightly. In their closing arguments, the Prosecution asserted that some Defences, in their final briefs, used linguistic gymnastics and a selective presentation of evidence. Your Honours, in the case of Valentin Coric, the Prosecution did all that and more. It ignored the statements of their own witnesses when it didn't suit them. The same documents were interpreted in different ways, depending on which one of the accused it pertained to. They fabricated facts that were not to be found in the documents. This is not the way one acts who struggles for international justice and the rights of victims. That is the way one acts if he or she wants victory at all costs. The Coric Defence, during its closing arguments, will show, by presenting several examples, that these are not merely hollow words. In their final brief, in paragraphs 982, 993, 1039, and in their closing arguments, the Prosecution, in order to show that my client was committed to the project of some Greater Croatia, quoted part of a publication that says that people were selected for the military police who were faithful to the Croatian idea and the homeland. The document I'm referring to is P8550. Whenever the Prosecution, in their final brief, tried to prove this thesis, it relies on this very document, one document only. The Prosecution does so because no other proof can be found in over 10.000 documents that have been presented in this trial, and they were unable to find anything else even in the statements of hundreds of witnesses. The Prosecution ignores the answer of a protected witness, who is questioned what this Croatian idea is that is mentioned in this publication, although no other witness has testified about that. The transcript pages are 51316 through 51318. And the witness said that in 1992, when the war started in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the homeland he was fighting for was Bosnia-Herzegovina. He added that the Croatian idea for the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina meant that they should be one of three equal and constituent peoples. The witness said that was the way he understood it and that it cannot be understood differently. Your Honours, it doesn't really matter how the Prosecutor or the Defence interpret documents pertaining to that period. What matters is the fact how the witnesses interpret those documents and how they interpreted them at the time. My learned friend Mr. Stringer said that it is not as clear as to how many Muslims would have been partisan to that idea which, according to the Prosecutor, was a condition for a job with the military police. My learned friend Mr. Stringer has probably failed to acknowledge that in this case, there is ample evidence about the fact how many Muslims there were in various units of the military police during the relevant period of the indictment. The Prosecutor has failed to acknowledge that Witness Andabak, on transcript pages 50949 through 50950, said that in the battalion that he commanded, there were 30 per cent Muslims, which, in numerical terms, meant a hundred men. The commander of the 2nd Light Assault Battalion was Muslim. Another witness, on transcript page 51318, said that in another military police unit, at first there were between 30 and 40 Muslims and some dozen Serbs, and later on that there were over 50 Muslims and anything between 10 and 15 Serbs. Witness Desnica, a Defence witness, in his statement, 5D5109, paragraph 9, was recorded as having said that Muslims and Croats alike attended military training or police training. I would like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to documents P2970 and P4850. Your Honours, all of those proves that Muslims in the military police understood the terms "Croatian idea" and "homeland" in the same way as the protected witness mentioned before, and not in the way interpreted by the Prosecutor. This also shows that Valentin Coric shared the opinion of the protected witness. Otherwise, he would not have put forth a Muslim as the commander of a light assault battalion. This is, Your Honour, the first example to show that the Prosecutor, when he doesn't really have any proof for his arguments, instead of proof which exists, offers to the Trial Chamber their own unproven and unfounded interpretations of the documents. In their final brief and in their closing arguments, in paragraph 982 and 986, the Prosecution for the first time tried to extend the alleged criminal responsibility of Mr. Coric by referring to his appointment to the duty as a minister of the interior in November 1993, as well as all of his other appointments within the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna throughout 1994 and 1995. It is inappropriate and too late for the Prosecution to offer arguments that did not exist in the indictment, arguments which were not presented during trial. It is too late to do it now. Both the indictment and the pre-trial brief limited the scope of Coric's alleged criminal responsibility to a period up to November 1993, and during that period they limited his responsibility as the chief of the Administration of Military Police, and you can find this in paragraphs 12 and 17.5 of the indictment. The Prosecution ignores the fact that as the minister of the interior, Coric demanded the return of the civilian police from the front-line. He wanted them to return in order to be able to fight crime. This is corroborated by document P6837. The Prosecutor also ignores the fact that Coric continued performing certain duties in Bosnia and Herzegovina even after the war, or, rather, after the Dayton Accords. He was a cantonal minister of the interior as well as the deputy minister for civilian affairs in Sarajevo. This is corroborated by document P9053. These appointments demonstrate that Mr. Coric was a professional and not somebody who was rewarded for crimes against non-Croats. In their final brief, the Prosecution refers to several meetings attended by Mr. Coric or at which his name was mentioned. The Prosecution requests from the Trial Chamber to arrive at a conclusion, based on those meetings, that Coric was a part of some alleged criminal plan. In paragraphs 982 and 986 of the Prosecution's final brief, the Prosecution claims that Coric was rewarded for his leading role in the so-called Herceg-Bosna project, and that his appointment as the Ministry of the Interior minister was approved by Tudjman, Boban and Prlic. As far as the leading role of Coric is concerned, I would like to point out that there are documents on file which show that he attended no more than four meetings of the HVO government. As you can see from the documents P4111, P4275, P5799 and 2D8454, the only reason why Coric was present at those four meetings was his duty to report about joint operations by the military and civilian police in their fight against crime, operations that were undertaken and which were planned. It arises clearly from the minutes of those meetings that the participants in the meetings, instead of discussing any kind of Herceg-Bosna criminal project, they actually discussed the need for further empowerment of the civilian and military police forces and creation of such an operative plan according to which the civilian and military police forces would work together with a view to fighting and stopping crime. The four meetings which were held with a view to fight crime as efficiently as possible, and if at those four meetings Mr. Coric had contributed to any kind of project, such a project cannot be defined as illegal or criminal. His appointment as the minister of the interior, which was based on his role played at the HVO meetings concerning his efforts to prevent crimes, certainly makes a lot of sense. The Prosecutor's negative conclusion, which arises from the same meetings, does not have any logical basis and doesn't make sense. As concerns the meeting illustrated by document P6581, it should be emphasised that it is clear from the minutes of the meeting that Tudjman was hardly aware of Valentin Coric's existence. At that meeting, Mr. Prlic stated that Coric was currently the head of the military police and that he enjoyed a lot of trust among the troops. In this case, we did not see any proof that would either confirm or disprove the alleged statement by Mr. Prlic concerning the trust of the army. The Prosecutor also refers to document P2099, quoted in paragraph 984 of their final brief. The Prosecutor claims that Coric also enjoyed support by Ivan Jarnjak. It also stems from the transcript that Tudjman again didn't know who Valentin Coric was or at least didn't know too well, and that Jarnjak's support was based only on the fact that that gentleman, during that meeting, said that him and Coric used to bump into each other in their karate club. It clearly arises from the documents that Coric did not attend any of the two meetings and that there is no single piece of evidence that would lead to a conclusion that he was ever familiar with the contents of those meetings. In their final brief, the Prosecutor on several occasions, for example, in paragraphs 11, 236 and 1003, refers to a meeting which was attended by Mr. Coric and General Praljak. The document number is P1788. During their closing argument, the Praljak Defence already objected to the authenticity and credibility of the handwritten notes. They challenged their authenticity, and we're not going to go over the same arguments again. In that part, we would like to join General Praljak's Defence. Moreover, there is no link between Coric's presence at that meeting and his participation with regard to the words uttered at that meeting by Mr. Praljak. At that meeting, Coric answered questions about the new organisation and the numerical strength of the military police. And with this regard, he stated that the military police would adhere to their former ways until a new agreement is reached. Valentin Coric's words were not part of a political speech. They also did not present an expression of any criminal intent. The Defence would like to remind the Trial Chamber that General Praljak, in his testimony, in answering questions by the honourable Judge Antonetti, said that he had never engaged in any political talks with Coric, nor was he ever familiar with Coric's political views. You can find those words on page T-41499 of the transcript. In paragraph 364 of their final brief, the Prosecutor claims that Jadranko Prlic, in his statement, document P9078, provided to the investigator of this Tribunal, referred to Coric as a clerical fascist. In that way, he ranked him among the group of people close to Tudjman and thus responsible for the war crimes committed by the HVO. Your Honours, this is simply not true. There is no place in that statement where Jadranko Prlic referred to Valentin Coric as a clerical fascist. Everything you can find in the document is the fact that Prlic and Coric did have some misgivings and disagreements. Your Honours, none of the aforementioned documents shows that Valentin Coric had any kind of opinion, any kind of a political view, which would be in favour of the secession of the HZ-HB from Bosnia and Herzegovina and the creation of some sort of a Greater Croatia. My learned friend Mr. Stringer, at the beginning of his closing argument, referred to the judgements in the Kvocka and Krajisnik cases and claimed that Coric's Defence had erroneously said that Mr. Coric could not be convicted for his participation in a joint criminal enterprise if his command responsibility was not simultaneously established pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute. Although it is true that these two legal forms of responsibility, pursuant to Article 7(3) and for JCE 7(1) [as interpreted] are different, like in any other case, that responsibility for the JCE pursuant to Article 7(1) must be established using concrete facts in the case; in other words, before the Trial Chamber. In the Kvocka case quoted by the Prosecutor, the accused were charged not only with ordering crimes to be committed, and orders being given to their subordinates, but also participating in those same crimes. In the Krajisnik case, there were also concrete facts which led to the judgement the way it was handed down. However, let's come back to the Prosecutor's case against Valentin Coric, because this is precisely what the Trial Chamber has to take into account, and you will see why we are claiming here that a responsibility, through Mr. Coric's participation in the joint criminal enterprise, cannot be proven if at the same time Coric's command role over the military police was not proven. In the appeal judgement in the Kvocka case quoted by the Prosecutor, paragraph 28 reads: [In English] "If the Prosecution relies on the theory of joint criminal enterprise, then the Prosecutor must plead the purpose of the enterprise, the identity of the participants, and the nature of the accused's participation in the enterprise." [Interpretation] In paragraph 33 of the same judgement, the Appeals Chamber elaborates that statement and says: [In English] "The Trial Chamber can only convict the accused of crimes which are charged in the indictment." [Interpretation] Why, in their final brief, the Prosecutor did not invoke the part of the indictment with relation to Mr. Coric, in relation to Mr. Coric? Your Honours, if we look at the indictment, paragraphs 12 and 17.5(A) to (N), in the pre-trial brief, the same paragraphs, the nature and way of participation in the JCE that Valentin Coric is charged with, we actually see that the Prosecution asserted that Coric, based on military -- based on command responsibility in the military police, participated in the JCE. That is why we assert that the problem with ascertaining Coric's command line intertwines with the issue of ascertaining his participation in the JCE. In the second amended indictment, in the part which has to do with Mr. Coric, it only states that he had de jure and de facto command and control over HVO military police. The Prosecutor could now conclude that he should have presented a better or different case against Mr. Coric. However, they're stuck with what they had said previously. In predominating jurisprudence, where the Prosecution need not prove that there was a superior-subordinate relation between the accused and physical perpetrators or indirect perpetrators, they have to prove that the accused held at least some kind of authority position that could have incited another to commit a crime following an order by the accused. This thesis is further corroborated by the judgement in the Milutinovic case in paragraph 87. In our final brief, paragraphs 67 to 72, we presented a detailed analysis about who it is exactly that the Prosecution asserts were Coric's subordinates, and in the pages following that we explained in detail whether Mr. Coric had a command role. And this is the topic I am going to cover in the next part of my presentation. The Prosecution and Petkovic Defence, in their final brief, offer several different theories about who, when, and how, commanded the military police. Let me cite a few examples. In paragraph 988, the Prosecution asserts that Coric commanded the military police, administratively and operationally. In paragraph 683, the Prosecution submits that Praljak's subordinates, including the military police, respected his superior authority. In paragraph 684, the Prosecution submits that Praljak had command responsibility over the military police, which had been re-subordinated to him by Boban and Stojic for combat operations. In paragraph 686, the Prosecution submits that Praljak commanded the entire spectrum of work of the military police, not only their participation in combat operations. Petkovic's Defence, in paragraphs 96 and 97 of their final brief, state that the chief of the Main Staff commanded the military police only when it was re-subordinated to him. In paragraph 99, the Petkovic Defence state that the commander of the Military Police Battalion in the operational zone was subordinated to the operational zone commander, in terms of regular military police tasks, and to the Military Police Administration when professional activities were in question. In paragraph 103, the Petkovic Defence state that the regular military police tasks were not within the remit of the chief of the Main Staff, and that it was because of that, those military commanders were subordinated to the head of the Department of Defence, in terms of regular military policing tasks. In paragraph 106, the Petkovic Defence submit that in relation to the military police units within operational zones and brigades, there was a double chain of command leading up to the military commander and the chief of the SIS or to the Military Police Administration. In several paragraphs of Defence 4D, such as paragraphs 99, 100, 106 and 204, they assert that the military police administration commanded the military police. Your Honours, different theories, which actually represent a Plan A, a Plan B, or a Plan C, and so on, indicate that the party offering so many different theories actually lacks any evidence to prove beyond a reasonable doubt any of them. The Coric Defence, as is well known in this courtroom, throughout the five years of this trial and in its final brief, defended only one thesis. The Coric Defence need not bother to construe different theories depending on which turn the case takes because we based our arguments on the evidence presented; not only documentary evidence, but also based on witness testimony. Our thesis, which is what I'm going to remind the Chamber about in the continuation of my closing argument, were confirmed not only by the witnesses of the Defence 5D, but also by Prosecution witnesses as well as the witnesses of the Defences of Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Praljak. Your Honours, concerning commanding over the military police, the Coric Defence submits that the evidence in this case indicate the following: The units of the military police were organised in five battalions, four of which had their respective operational zone, and only one did not have a standing territorial deployment. This is confirmed by documents P936, P128, P957, and it was also confirmed by the following witnesses: Witness Andabak, at transcript pages 50906 to 50908, 50912, 50915, 50917 to 50918, and 50920; CC, a Prosecution witness, at transcript pages 10452, 10453, and 10458; EA, another Prosecution witness, at transcript pages 24875 to 24880, and 24884 to 24886; OTP Witness C at transcript pages 22520, 22521, and 22524 to 22527; as well as NO, a witness of Defence 5D in his statement which was admitted in this case as 5D5110 in its fourth paragraph. The single battalion, without a standing territorial deployment, could be sent to a specific operational zone following Mr. Coric's order. In order to be able to do that, he had to receive an order from the Main Staff which had previously been approached by the operational zone commander to do so. This is confirmed by documents 5D4040, 5D4030, 5D4039, 5D440, and P5478. It was also confirmed by several witnesses, such as Witness Andabak, a Defence witness of Defence team 5D, at pages 50911 and 50912; an OTP Witness C at transcript pages 22524 to 22527; EA, another OTP witness, at transcript pages 24879 to 24881. That situation was changed towards late July, but I will address that issue at a later stage. In their daily tasks, the military police battalions were commanded by operational zone commanders. This is confirmed by documents 5D5095, 5D4374, 5D4375, P2534, P4063, 3D2584, 3D1785, 5D2195, 5D4380, 5D1054, P2548, P2640, P3135, 5D4392, 5D3052, 5D3046, P1913, P1972, 5D3044, 5D3019, P5731, P3593, P5411, 3D798, P781, 5D2102, P4251, P1238, P2836, and P1359. Since I don't have sufficient time to do so, I am unable to list all such documents here. However, this issue was also confirmed by the following witnesses: OTP Witness EA at transcript page 24876 to 24877; OTP Witness CC at transcript page 10458 to 22527 and 22451 to 22453 -- sorry, I apologise to the interpreters. I seem to have skipped a line. OTP Witness C at transcript pages 22524-22527 and 22451-22453. I apologise to the interpreters, and will go back two lines because I forgot to read out one witness. OTP Witness CC at transcript page 10458, Defence Witness, 5D, NO at transcript pages 51181 to 51182, Defence Witness, 4D, Petkovic at transcript pages 50249 to 50254 and 50260 to 50261; Defence Witness, 4D, Pavlovic at transcript pages 46905 to 46907; Defence Witness, 5D, Andabak at transcript pages 50906, 50907, 50917, 50918, 50934, 50935, 50939 to 50942, 50950, and 50951; Defence Witness, 5D, Vidovic at transcript page 51512. There were also certain situations in which a commander -- the commander of an operational zone re-subordinated individual companies or parts thereof to the commanders of his own brigades or to the battalions contained in those brigades. This is confirmed by documents 5D2102, and P02846. It was also confirmed by Defence Witness, 5D, Andabak at transcript pages 50934 and 50935. Your Honours, daily tasks of the military police include all those affairs which are part of the scope of work of the military police. It is confirmed by documents 5781, P635, P4063, P1238, P1359, P2836, P4251, P2534, 3D2584, 3D1785, 5D2102, 5D5095, 5D4374, and 5D4375.
