utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The first document in this sequence is P781. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] It was also confirmed by the following witnesses: Defence Witness, 4D, Pavlovic at transcript page 46905; Prosecution Witness C at transcript page 22325; Defence Witness, 5D, Andabak at transcript pages 50917 and 50918; and Defence Witness, 4D, Petkovic at transcript pages 50232 to 50260. I will enumerate but a few of those daily tasks of the military police: Securing facilities, bringing in deserters, control of entry and exit in an area of responsibility, detection of crime, internal security of military prisons, and taking part in providing security for POWs. It is confirmed by documents P1148, P143, and P837. It was also confirmed by the following witnesses: Defence Witness, 4D, Petkovic at transcript pages 50232 to 50236, and 50349 to 50261 [as interpreted]; OTP Witness EA at transcript page 24878 and 24879. Your Honours, the daily tasks of the military police are regular tasks that the military police carries out anywhere in the world. The Coric Defence, therefore, simply fails to understand about which professional activities the Petkovic Defence speaks in paragraph 99 of their final brief. Apart from the active military police about which I have just spoken, there was also the brigade military police. The brigade military police was organised in platoons, and every brigade had one such platoon in their structure. The brigade military police was in all matters subordinated to the brigade commanders, just as any other unit belonging to that brigade. The brigade commanders commanded the brigade platoons. The brigade commanders selected personnel for these platoons as well as appointed and -- appointed members of these platoons. Brigade commanders were supposed to launch, and they did launch, disciplinary proceedings against members of the brigade platoons of the military police. This is confirmed by documents P4262, 5D538, P1099, P4413, P990, P2595, 5D5106, 5D5107. This was also confirmed by witnesses: The 5D Witness, Andabak, on transcript pages 50913 through 50928; the 4D Defence, Petkovic, on transcript pages 50226 through 50229; Prosecution Witness CC on transcript pages 10449 and 10458; Prosecution Witness C on transcript pages 22525 through 22527; and the 3D and 4D Witness Tokic on transcript page 45507. Military commanders commanded the units of the military police, no matter if we're talking about the brigade or the active military police in combat operations. This was confirmed by the following Prosecution witnesses: Witness CC on transcript page 10458; Witness EA on transcript pages 24876 and 24877, as well as 24879 through 24880; then there is Prosecution Witness C on transcript pages 22520 and 22540 through 22541; the next is the 3D Witness Skender on transcript page 45241; the 4D Witness Pavlovic on transcript pages 46894 through 46895, and 46905; the 3D Witness General Praljak on transcript page 42692; the 4D Witness Petkovic on transcript pages 49791 through 49795; the 5D Witness Andabak on transcript pages 50933 through 50934; then the 5D Witness NO in his statement which was admitted as 5D5110 in paragraphs 4 and 5. Your Honours, throughout the period covered by the indictment while Valentin Coric was chief of the MP Administration, the military police, in its daily tasks as well as in combat operations, was commanded by military commanders in their respective zones of responsibility. That was confirmed by 5D Witness Andabak on transcript pages 50909 and the following. Why was that the case, Your Honours? Any operative zone commander and, within that operative zone, any brigade commander had their respective zone of responsibility. The zone of responsibility has a certain depth and width, and includes not only the front-line, but also a stretch of territory behind it. The depth is determined based on the security assessment of the area commander, and it can go up to 10 or 15 kilometres. In one operative zone, where the zone of responsibility of the commander of a brigade ends, the zone of responsibility of the commander of another brigade begins. That is confirmed by documents P4819 and P3135. It was also confirmed by witnesses: The 3D and 4D Witness Tokic on transcript page 45343; and the 5D Witness Andabak on transcript pages 50943. The commander of a zone was the person who knew best what was happening in his zone. He knew where enemy positions were. He knew what the security situation was like. He knew what the points of entry and points of exit into or from his zone of responsibility were and where he will set up check-points. He was the one who knew which forces he had at his disposal. The following witnesses confirmed that: The 5D Witness Andabak on transcript pages 50943 and the following; Defence Witness Skender, that is, 3D Witness Skender, on transcript pages 45310 and 45283; then 5D Witness Vidovic on transcript page 51453; the 3D and 4D Witness Tokic on transcript pages 45336 through 45547; then there is 2D Witness Bandic on transcript page 38105. That is why, Your Honours, this commander was the one who decided daily which part of his forces, including the military police, would do what. At daily briefings which had to be attended and, indeed, were attended by the commanders of the military police, among others, assigned tasks and received reports. That was confirmed by 5D Witness Andabak on transcript pages 50932 through 50934, then 50940 and 51146. That commander received written reports from all his units, including the military police. That is confirmed by documents P970, 5D4385, P4063, P2836, P1359, P377, P458. There have also been witnesses who confirmed that: Prosecution Witness C on transcript page 22323; 5D Witness Andabak on transcript pages 50931 through 50959; and 5D Witness NO in his statement which was admitted into evidence as 5D5110. It is the fifth paragraph of that statement. What is the role of the commander in his zone of responsibility? We can tell by reviewing document P3135. Colonel Obradovic states in this document that he issues that order pursuant to the unlimited authority that he received by civilian and military structures in keeping with the widening of his zone of responsibility. The following situation also proves that the commanders of operative zones had effective control over the military police in their zones. There are several orders issued by Valentin Coric to military police in the case file, and these orders do not relate to professional structures, staffing, or familiarising with legislation. In such orders that relate to military police tasks, Valentin Coric in the preamble invokes the Main Staff or some other high-ranking body. Why does he do that if they are his subordinates? Why doesn't he simply say, Do it, as he does in case of instructions? The only logical conclusion is the following: Because these military policemen cannot carry out the order unless they are allowed to do so by the commander of the operative zone who commands them on a daily basis. And the superior of that operative zone commander is the Main Staff, so if Valentin Coric invokes an order of the Main Staff, the commander of the operative zone will not be able to prevent the implementation of that order. This confirmed by documents 5D4282, P2020, P875, and P864. This thesis of the Coric Defence is confirmed by the order on check-points, which is co-signed by General Praljak, the head of the Department of Defence, and Valentin Coric. I'm referring to document P875. The same document also has an alternative number, and that is P876. During his testimony, Mr. Praljak said that he co-signed that order for it to have more weight. Your Honours, this order was issued to the military police. This is recorded on transcript page 40539. There is a sentence in the structure of the military police that is used both by the Prosecution, in their brief, and also by the Petkovic Defence. It says that the Military Police Administration is in charge of and commands military police units. At first glance, this sentence may be in contradiction with what I've just said, and I'm sure that Your Honours remember that this caused much debate during this trial. Probably this situation would remain unresolved to this day if -- hadn't we heard witnesses in this case, and the witnesses, loudly and clearly, under oath and without second thought, said to this Trial Chamber that the military police, in its daily tasks as well as in combat operations, was commanded by military commanders, rather than the Military Police Administration. This is confirmed by many documents, of which I have mentioned only a few. The witnesses confirmed that the Military Police Administration was responsible for staffing, the provision of MP equipment, training, and disciplinary proceedings against military police members. This is confirmed by 5D Witness Andabak on transcript pages 50906 and the following. This was also confirmed by NO in his statement which was admitted into evidence as 5D5110. Who commands the military police, and how, and what kind of role the Military Police Administration has in this context is best illustrated by Judge Trechsel's question to Defence Witness Skender and the answer this witness provided. Judge Trechsel said: "I don't think it is -- this is possible. We need to clarify this. If there are two commanders who can give orders, that both are entitled to do this, this would appear rather disorderly. Could you not clarify this for us, please, in administrative terms? The military policemen were still part of the Military Police Administration, whereas as far as their work on the ground, while they are part of the brigade, it is only the brigade commander who tells them what they must do on the battle-field?"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "A. Yes, that's right. "Q. I think this had made things clear, and we have been able to iron out some of these differences we had. Thank you." [Interpretation] End quote. And now I will just briefly say something about one part of administrative authorities, those that the Military Police Administration had vis-a-vis military police units. The chief of the Military Police Administration, de jure, was in a position to appoint company commanders and lower-ranking officers in the units of active military police. When it comes to the battalion commanders, he only -- he could only propose appointments. This is illustrated, for example, by document P143. The candidate for battalion commander in any operative zone was pre-selected by a commission. For example, a commission for deciding on the candidates for the commander of the 1st Battalion, one of the members was a representative of the Main Staff, whereas the commander of the operative zone was a member of a commission appointing commanders for other active battalions. This was confirmed by Witness Andabak on page T-50914 as well as document P960. However, the fact that some commanders may have been selected unbeknownst to Valentin Coric, and the examples for that are documents P3409 and P4494. The example of Mijo Jelic is the best illustration of the extent to which the Administration of the Military Police de facto participated in the staffing policy. Mijo Jelic, Your Honour, was the commander of the 1st Light Assault Battalion on the 2nd of July, 1993. On that day, pursuant to Miljenko Lasic's order, and he was the commander of the South-East Herzegovina Operative Zone, he was appointed as the commander of one sector in the city of Mostar. Nobody consulted Valentin Coric prior to that. Nobody even formally informed him about that. This is proven by document P3117. On the 6th of August, 1993, the chief of the Main Staff appointed Mijo Jelic as the commander of the defence of the city of Mostar. Nobody consulted Valentin Coric. Nobody sought his opinion yet again. This is proven by document P3983. It is true, Your Honours, that at that point Mijo Jelic was a military policeman. However, when it comes to his destiny, Valentin Coric could have as big a say as he could have if at that point in time Mijo Jelic was, for example, a postman. Let me give you another example as to what kind of authority Valentin Coric had, or better said, didn't have over the military police. Valentin Coric wanted to discipline a member of the military police. However, General Praljak prevented him from doing that. General Praljak said that he was the one who had operative command over that particular military policeman. You will see proof of that in documents P3068 and 5D4394. The Prosecution and the Petkovic and Praljak Defence teams claim that it was only from the 28th of July, 1993, pursuant to Valentin Coric, seen in document P3778, the military police was engaged and re-subordinated to military commanders. In pleading their case, these Defence teams go even further and say that the military police were subordinated to them for a very brief period of time and for very specific tasks. Your Honours, I have just listed the names of all the witnesses who confirmed that throughout all that time, the commanders of the military police were military commanders, both when they were engaged in combat as well as when they were performing their daily duties. Your Honours, no order on re-subordination had to exist in order for military commanders to be in command, and there is a simple reason why such an order did not have to exist. The military police were already re-subordinated to military commanders by their organisation. Document P3778 is not a document testifying to re-subordination. This is what it is: Before this order was issued, Valentin Coric, pursuant to an order of the Main Staff, had to move the military police from one zone to another, because they had their own permanent territorial deployment. Likewise, he sent the 1st Battalion, pursuant to the Main Staff orders, wherever the Main Staff wanted to send the battalion. This order which Valentin Coric did not issue of his own will, but rather pursuant to an order that he had already received from the Main Staff, completely throws out Valentin Coric from the story. From that moment, military commander, headed by the Main Staff, deployed military police units wherever they wanted and whenever they wanted. This is confirmed by the fact that all witnesses which I have already mentioned, in addition to Praljak and Petkovic, confirmed that the de facto system of command over the military police functioned equally throughout all that time in all of the operative zones. The following examples that show that military commanders commanded over the military police, these are the examples for the orders of military commanders for the daily tasks of the military police: P3039, P3135, P2030, P2548, P1359, P2836 - I apologise, Your Honours. Could you please bear with me for a moment - P2640, P1913, 5D2195, 5D4040, 5D3044, 5D3046, 5D3048, 5D3052, 5D3019, 5D1054, 5D4392, 5D4030, 5D5095, 5D4374, 5D4380. And now the example showing that even before the order by Mr. Valentin Coric was issued, commanded over military police in combat: 3D1785, 5D2102, 5D4387, 5D4385, 5D4382, 5D4375, 5D4376, 5D4377. And now examples of orders issued by the Main Staff to the military police via the Military Police Administration for their daily tasks: P323, P708, 5D4282. There was no single order that went straight from the Main Staff via the Military Police Administration for combat activities. And now examples of orders issued by the Main Staff, sent directly to the military police without the involvement of the Military Police Administration for daily tasks: P638, P377, P2534, P1344, P933, P458. And now examples of the Main Staff orders sent directly to the military police for combat operations, without the involvement of the Military Police Administration: P1888, P3117, P3128. Your Honours, this may be a good time for our next break, I believe.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] We continue. You have the floor. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Another part of the Prosecutor's case, argued in their final brief in paragraph 1058, as well as in their closing argument, as well as in the Petkovic final brief in paragraph 95, is the fact that Valentin Coric received combat reports. Your Honours, we assert that Valentin Coric did not receive a single combat report. We also claim that he did not issue a single combat order. A combat report has to contain the following: Information about the enemy, including the enemy's activities; deployment and future intentions; information about one's own forces, including activities in the course of the previous day; the technical deployment problems and how they were dealt with; losses; requirements with regard to the materiel and technical equipment; as well as other requirements. All this information has to be very precise. This is proven by documents 5D4385 and P1915. A combat order or an order for combat has to contain the following: Information about the enemy; information about the enemy forces; information about their technical equipment and deployment; deployment of one's own forces and their precise combat tasks; the description of signals and communications; the plan of movements; the designation of command posts and strategic points; the designation of artillery support; instructions and tasks which concern the security organs and intelligence organs; instructions and tasks for the engineers as well as the logistics men. This is proven by documents P3246, 5D4387, P1933, P1932, P4719, P4777, P3117, and 4D1700. There is no evidence in the case file proving that Valentin Coric ever received such reports or ever issued such orders. In paragraph 998, the Prosecutor claims that Valentin Coric personally carried out the inspection of the front-line in Mostar, and that after that he was the one who ordered that reinforcements should arrive, and how they would be deployed. Of the nine documents invoked by the Prosecutor, in that only one has something to do with the specific situation. This is document P5657. And now could we go into private session for a couple of minutes, please.

utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Prosecution claims that Valentin Coric received, personally, to his attention all the reports that were issued by every single military policeman of the HVO. The Coric Defence has described at great length in their final brief the system of reporting within the military police. Therefore, we will not belabour the point now. I will just briefly say that evidence on file and testimonies of witnesses demonstrate that when it came to regular reporting, in case of active battalions, only summary reports could reach Valentin Coric via the operative duty service. Summaries compiled by the duty operations officers, who included into those summary reports whatever events they deemed important. This was confirmed by Witnesses Andabak, a Defence witness, on transcript page 50931; Prosecution Witness C on transcript page 22560. This is also corroborated by documents P420, P423, and P6722. Only in very rare cases, only in very exceptional situations, were reports sent straight to Valentin Coric. As far as the brigade military police were concerned, the brigade military police never sent their reports to the Military Police Administration or to the military police battalions. The brigade military police sent their reports to brigades. This, for example, was confirmed by Witness Andabak on transcript page 50929. Another example to corroborate that is document P4110. How come that only the reports of the 5th Battalion of the Military Police mention the activities of the brigade military police in their area is a special subject which was dealt with by the Coric Defence in their closing brief, so we will not belabour the point again. The Petkovic Defence, in paragraph 106 of their final brief, assert that with regard to the military police, there existed a double chain of command, as well as that there were problems in commanding the military police. They invoke two documents and a number of transcript pages from the testimony of General Praljak. On those pages, there is no mention made about this assertion by the Petkovic Defence. Witness NO was shown these two documents, and he stated that no military commander ever mentioned to him any double command chain with regards to the military police. No one ever mentioned to him any problems which would have to do with commanding the military police. We'd like to stress that that witness, according to his own testimony, personally knew basically all military commanders of the HVO. It was recorded at transcript pages 51326 and 51328. Besides, in Mr. Petkovic's report for six months -- for a period of six months in 1993, an entire spectrum of problems is outlined, but not a single one has to do with the military police. It is document P3642. Your Honours, I'd like to draw your attention to document P4792. In that document, the chief of the Main Staff ordered the commander of the North-Western Herzegovina Operational Zone, Mr. Siljeg, not to let through UNPROFOR vehicles, UN vehicles, and UNHCR vehicles through the check-points, but that it should be done in a way so as to suggest that it was done by the MPs manning the check-points of their own accord. Your Honours, the Coric Defence submits that this is the best example to illustrate how and why fairy-tales were constructed about the double command chain and the recalcitrance of the military police. At the beginning, I said that I will use the many examples to show, inter alia, how the Prosecutor ignored their own witnesses and testimonies when it was not to their advantage. They did so precisely in this case when they were trying to show that Valentin Coric and the Military Police Administration commanded the units of the military police. Leaving aside the fact that the Prosecutor ignored a number of Defence witnesses and their testimonies, even though some of them appeared as Defence witnesses, contradicting the thesis put forth by the representative Defences, Your Honours, the Prosecutors in this case ignored their own witnesses, C, CC, and EA. In spite of all statements by Prosecution witnesses, as well as Defence witnesses, the Prosecution puts forth their thesis that Coric commanded the military police by trying to show that through three witnesses, Witness E and the accused Petkovic and Praljak. It is only good fortune for the Prosecution that the accused testified. Otherwise, after an investigation which took a number of years, and five years of proceedings in this courtroom, and after a few hundred witnesses, the only witness who could address that thesis would have been Witness E. First, I'd like to deal briefly with the credibility of Witness E. Without any hesitation, the Prosecution declared the Coric Defence Witness NO a war criminal, and all that about a man who has never been charged, let alone sentenced, for a war crime. On the other hand, without any hesitation, in order to corroborate their thesis, they relied (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: (redacted). I'd like to remind Your Honours that there are exhibits confirming that in this case, which are 2D511, 2D512, and 2D513. Having analysed the testimony of the accused Petkovic and Praljak, which was used in order to prove the Prosecution thesis against my client, the Prosecution, in their final brief, said the following; paragraph 3: [In English] "This is especially true of the testimony of the accused Praljak and Petkovic, who lied repeatedly when they were not evading questions on important issues. Their self-serving testimony is entitled to little weight." [Interpretation] Paragraph 836: [In English] "Praljak lied under oath." [Interpretation] Paragraph 839: [In English] "Praljak repeatedly lied to the Trial Chamber during weeks of his sworn testimony, both in direct and cross-examination. When he was not lying, he was evading giving direct answers to questions." [Interpretation] Paragraph 840: [In English] "Later in his testimony, Praljak distinguished between vital truth and factual truth. It is not clear which of these varieties of truth Praljak employed while testifying." [Interpretation] Paragraph 862: [In English] "Petkovic had great difficulty giving direct, truthful and candid answers during his testimony." [Interpretation] Paragraph 900: [In English] "This Petkovic evasion again holds no water." [Interpretation] Paragraph 935: [In English] "Petkovic assurances cannot be believed." [Interpretation] Similar or same qualifications the Prosecutor repeats in paragraphs 650, footnote 1502, paragraph 746, 837, 838, 864, 867, 870, 873, 902, 905, 908, 909, 936, and 939. Although in all these paragraphs the Prosecutor qualified the two accused as notorious liars, they did not think twice before using their testimony to confirm their thesis against my client, Valentin Coric, and all that despite the fact that the testimony in question is contradictory with the testimony of other Prosecution witnesses as well as Defence witnesses of the same accused, Petkovic and Praljak. This, Your Honours, is a very good example showing that the Prosecution, depending on who the target is, offers different interpretations of testimony, assigning them different probative value. Your Honours, there is a possibility that a witness, though not credible, sometimes may say something truthful. However, in order to be trusted, what he said needs to be confirmed by someone credible, someone that this Court can trust. However, if that witness speaks differently from all the other witnesses who the Court can believe, and if such testimony assists the person in question to be personally exculpated, such a person cannot and must not be believed. The Prosecution, in their final brief, say that Valentin Coric hid behind his desk, pretending to be a clerk, a bureaucrat. Your Honours, Valentin Coric did not hide then and is not hiding now. At the time, Valentin Coric was prevented from taking part in the appointment of military policemen. He was prevented from instituting disciplinary procedures. I'd like to remind Your Honours that Valentin Coric requested the Main Staff to withdraw military policemen from the front-line. Proof of that is document P5471 and General Praljak's testimony, who stated that it was his decision not to meet that particular request by Coric. It was recorded on transcript pages 40988, 40989, 42523 to 42527. Your Honours, had Valentin Coric been the commander of the military police, he would have withdrawn those men. He would not have needed any -- Praljak's permission, nor would Mr. Praljak have been able to decide on that. Valentin Coric's Defence is not shying away. Our assertions are confirmed by evidence and credible witnesses. I'd like to move on to another topic now. The Prosecution, in paragraph 1036 of their final brief, assert that Valentin Coric was informed on the 30th of January, 1993, of the misconduct of the military police in Prozor. In doing so, the Prosecution invokes document P1362, in which the brigade commander of Rama, by the name of Zutic, states that no order was implemented unless the military police had its own interest in doing so. By the same token, mention is made of a problematic military policeman whose nickname was Banja Luka. Your Honours, first I'd like to draw your attention to an order of that same brigade commander, Mr. Zutic, dated the 27th of January, 1993, that is to say, three days prior, in which he states, by sending it to the military police: "I order that at military police check-points in the area of our municipality, the personnel staffing the check-points from the military police should be informed of the following: "1. No Muslim can traverse the area of this municipality; "2. Buses travelling through the area of the municipality should be controlled more carefully, and any Muslim found on board such buses should be removed; "3. Goods and cargo Muslims are trying to transfer through our municipality should be seized." This order is in force immediately, and the personnel at all check-points should be acquainted with it. Your Honours, this is document P1327. It is clear what the order in question is. The Coric Defence asserts that the military police conducted themselves in a legal fashion by not implementing this order. Your Honours, I'd like to remind you that in document P1362, referred to by the Prosecutor, the brigade commander mentioned the military policeman by the nickname of Banja Luka as a problematic person. In paragraph 1036, the Prosecution again asserts that this Banja Luka person was a military policeman. Your Honours, not only that he was never a military policeman, he was even declared unfit to serve the army, as can be seen in the criminal report submitted against him, which is document P4836. In paragraph 1037 of their final brief, the OTP assert that Miroslav Bralo was released from detention, although a criminal report was submitted against him for murder, with a view to including him in combat operations. The Coric Defence would like to retray [as interpreted] that the military police submitted a criminal report against that person for the murder of a Muslim, and following that report he was detained in the military prison Kaonik. It is clearly illustrated by P1405. The Kaonik Military Prison was not under the competence of neither the military police nor the Military Police Administration, and they had no say over who could be released from detention. The Kaonik Military Prison was under the authority of the Central Bosnia Operational Zone, as indicated by document P1478. In paragraph 1017 of their final brief, the Prosecution assert that Coric, on 25 October 1992, was informed by Siljeg, commander of the North-West Herzegovina Operational Zone, about criminal misconduct of the military police. In paragraph 1018, they continue the story by saying that four days later, which would be the 29th of October, a meeting was held in Ljubuski, attended by Coric, and that it was there where he was informed of that criminal conduct. Your Honours, first of all, that meeting, which is in document P1350, was not held four days later. It was three months later, in January 1993. In that document, there is no mention of either Siljeg or any criminal conduct by the military police. Quite the contrary, the military police was praised by those in attendance. The problems discussed there concerning crime were the technical issues the Crime Service was facing, which had nothing to do with criminal acts. In other words, to assert that some criminal conduct by the military police was discussed at the meeting is a simple fabrication. Let me return to Mr. Siljeg's report. Let me first refer to the document the Prosecution cites, and that is P648. This document doesn't deal with any sort of command conduct by the military police, which is seen from the reply to that document, which is 3D424. Instead, the document is about vehicles that the military police had taken from thieves and which it was returning to the rightful owners. This was confirmed by Witnesses Andabak and Praljak, and everything is explained in detail in paragraph 617 of our final brief. Now I would like to say a few words about the commander of the North-West Herzegovina Operative Zone, whom the Prosecution cites several times in their attempts to try to prove that the military police was involved in illegal conduct. This operative zone commander, Mr. Siljeg, is the same one the Prosecution points out in paragraph 880 of his final brief as an example of a commander who uses abusive language when referring to Muslims. This man, Your Honours, is the same one who, although he knows perfectly well that at that point in time he had prisoners in Prozor, lied to the Health Section of the Department of Defence that he doesn't have any, and he goes on to say, You have no right to issue orders to me. That can be seen in document P6203. That's the same man, Your Honours, who was tasked by the commander of the Main Staff not to let UNPROFOR, UN, and UNHCR vehicles pass and to misrepresent it as arbitrary conduct of the military police. That's document P4792. That man is the very same commander who, in the document, gives instructions to conceal dead bodies, which can be seen in document P1308. It's the same man who accuses the military police of stealing tanker-trucks from the convoy, although he knew that these tanker-trucks were in his possession. A longer story about this incident can be found in our closing -- in our final brief in paragraph 748. This is the same man, Your Honours, who follows orders to tidy up his prisoners before the Red Cross arrived. That's P4188. This, Your Honours, is the credible evidence that the Prosecution puts forward against the military police and Valentin Coric. But with who does this gentleman -- this commander have problems, Your Honours? He doesn't have a problem with Franjic, for example. He doesn't complain of him. Well, that's hardly surprising because that man, Franjic, is his own man, an earlier brigade commander turned military policeman, and when he was supposed to be arrested, the same Siljeg accepts him again as the brigade commander. The entire chronology is described in detail in our final brief in paragraphs 612 and 617. I will tell you who was a problem for Mr. Siljeg. Your Honours, it was Mr. Andabak who was a problem for him, the commander of the military police battalion that covered his operative zone. And who is Mr. Andabak? Mr. Zdenko Andabak continued his military career after the war in the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mr. Andabak became colonel of those armed forces, and he was commander of the Combat Simulation Centre under the Training and Doctrine Command. Mr. Andabak stated that on transcript pages 50904 and 50905, as well as in document 5D5084. Mr. Andabak couldn't have become an officer in the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina if there had been a shadow of doubt that he had ever committed a crime, especially a war crime against Muslims. I'm going to move on to another topic now. In their final brief, the Prosecution asserts that Valentin Coric commanded the Convicts Battalion and that Valentin Coric and the military police tolerated the criminal activities of the Convicts Battalion and its members. Under the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, it is impermissible for the Prosecution to put forward a new thesis for the first time now, after five years into the trial, in their final brief, and only now mention a new subordinate over whom Valentin Coric allegedly had authority. The jurisprudence of the Tribunal stipulates that all matters of substance shall be described in the indictment in detail, including all allegedly subordinate persons for whose acts the accused is -- was or is allegedly responsible under Article 7(3), in order for the accused to be informed what he can defend himself against. That is corroborated by various legal authorities who we cite in paragraph 6 and paragraphs 67 through 72 of our final brief. The indictment identifies as his subordinates only the military police of the HVO, and thus informs the accused Coric of his potential responsibility under Article 7(3). We can read that in paragraph 12. Thus, this change in the Prosecution case at the very end of the trial infringes upon the principle of a fair trial and the rights of the accused and must be refused by the Trial Chamber. In paragraph 1028, the Prosecution, citing a single document, for the first time in this trial asserts that Valentin Coric had authority over the Convicts Battalion and that he issued an order to them. Your Honours, the document which the Prosecution cites is P1517, and it is an order issued by Valentin Coric, but that order wasn't issued to the Convicts Battalion, but to the military police, although mention is made of the Convicts Battalion in the order. It can also be seen from the document that Valentin Coric here doesn't act on his own, but rather was ordered to issue this order. The Prosecution tried to corroborate their assertion that Valentin Coric tolerated the crimes of the Convicts Battalion without reacting to them. They used several documents to that end. They cite document P5477, which was sent to head of the Department of Defence. The same document, only sent to or addressed to the chief of Main Staff, is Exhibit 2D974. In this document, Mr. Vidovic from the Crime Service of the Military Police warns the then chief of Main Staff of all problems that they are facing due to crime and neglect of discipline in military units, including the problems these units are creating at the Heliodrom, and especially points out the situation in which the detained members of the Convicts Battalion were released following Tuta's orders. In the original document, as well as in the English translation, Vidovic calls these criminals heroes, but the word "heroes" is in inverted commas. In their final brief, paragraph 1034, the Prosecution, quoting from this document, leaves out the inverted commas, and thus totally changes the meaning of what Vidovic wrote and meant. This, Your Honour, is yet another example of misquoting evidence by the Prosecution. Based on that document, the Prosecution construes another thesis; namely, that Vidovic, although he's a member of the military police, contacts the Main Staff because he knows that he cannot expect help from Coric. The Prosecution here prefers to construe something like that rather than to accept the only logical conclusion to which anybody -- at which anybody reasonable will arrive. Your Honours, it is clear and logical that Vidovic contacted the Main Staff, because to Vidovic's understanding, the Main Staff was superior to the armed forces and, due to that fact, had the power and the authority to discipline Tuta, the commander of the Convicts Battalion. This was confirmed by Vidovic, himself, when he gave evidence before this Court so recorded on transcript pages 51644 and the following. The Prosecution construes the following from this, without any foundation: that Coric was the one who released criminals from prison to enable them to take part in combat operations. It is obvious from the document which I have just quoted or which I have just cited that those mentioned above were released pursuant to Tuta's rather than Coric's orders, and that the military police informed the Main Staff about that. Document P5891 contains another example in which Lasic, operative zone commander, orders the release of another group of soldiers from detention, and these soldiers were remanded in custody for a crime -- on criminal charges. Your Honours, there is not a single order issued by Valentin Coric along the same lines, namely, that criminals should be released. The Prosecution also, citing document P3928 in paragraph 1031, assert that it follows from one sentence of that document that the Convicts Battalion, pursuant to Coric's orders, enjoyed immunity from criminal prosecution. That is simply untrue, Your Honours, because the sentence in question can be interpreted either way. That is why it is irrelevant why this sentence is interpreted by either the Prosecution or the Defence. It is relevant how credible witnesses of that time interpret it. Witness Vidovic, in his evidence, explained that the criminal offences of members of various criminal groups were registered, not in order to tolerate their crimes, but in order to prepare a comprehensive police and judicial operation against these criminals. Various HVO bodies took part in these preparations, and this operation was eventually carried out. This was confirmed by Witness Bandic and by Witness NO. The Coric Defence has dealt with this in detail at paragraph 286 of its final brief, and there is no need for me to repeat what has already been mentioned there. About the allegations in paragraph 1033 of the Prosecution final brief about a particular incident, I would like to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to documents 5D2097, 5D2095, and P6893, as well as to the evidence given by Witness Vidovic on transcript pages 51495 through 51497. It follows from these documents that not only were criminal reports filed, but also an on-site investigation was conducted. We see that both the military police and the civilian police took part in the investigation, that the prosecutor was informed and so was the investigative judge. The Coric Defence asserts, and I will go into more detail later, that as of the moment when the Court and the Prosecutor's Office are informed of the case, the police no longer has any authority over the case. Instead, it's the investigative judge who has authority. To corroborate their thesis that Coric tolerated the crimes of ethnic cleansing, the Prosecution several times, both in their closing arguments and in their final brief, cite document P2802. In that report of the military police for 15 June 1993, under the heading "Crime," we can read the following: During the previous day, not one criminal offence was recorded, not one incident; only the ethnic cleansing of the town of persons of Muslim ethnicity has been recorded. From this sentence, the Prosecution somehow drew the conclusion that it proved that the military police considers ethnic cleansing not to be a crime. The Defence asserts that the Prosecution's conclusion is completely wrong and unfounded, and that is confirmed by documents P2769, P2574 and P2749. It's about this same case that is described in the document cited by the Prosecution. It can be seen from these documents that the military police in this particular case went out on the ground upon receiving a report that Stela and his soldiers were harassing Muslim civilians. It is also obvious that these criminals said that they had been ordered by their superior, Tuta. It can also be seen that the military police was looking for one of them. It is obvious that the situation was verging on armed conflict between the military police and the criminals. Your Honours, it is also obvious that the military police immediately reported to the Main Staff about the entire incident. Your Honours, it is clear that at that moment, the military police did whatever they could at that moment. The situation threatened to turn into an armed conflict between two military formations, of which one was acting on the orders of their superior, who was a criminal, and the orders were of a criminal nature. Everything was happening in the city among the civilians, and the only thing the military police could do at the moment was to inform the Main Staff. They could only hope for some assistance from their joint superior. That's why they addressed him. The Defence here would like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention that in one of the documents, it says that the military police was powerless, because instead of being engaged in proper policing, they had to man the lines. Your Honours, it is precisely because of this type of situation that Coric wanted the police to be withdrawn from the front-lines. The Prosecution offered a very ironical comment when they said that light assault battalions normally do not engage in criminal investigations. It is true, Your Honours, that they don't, they don't engage in criminal investigations. However, imagine a situation when you have only a few crime investigations [as interpreted] armed with nothing but pistols. They cannot encounter dangerous groups, they cannot arrest anybody. It is a notorious fact that in such cases, crime inspectors need the support of intervention police, and in this particular case, the intervention police would have been light assault battalions or units. Your Honours, would the military police have undertaken everything that they did, would they have issued several reports about this incident, if that incident had been something completely normal for them and if it had been something completely desirable? I'm sure that they wouldn't. Likewise, they would not have included the incident under "Crime" in document P2802 had they not considered the incident to be a crime. Every other interpretation, Your Honours, is nothing but an attempt to engage in some linguistic gymnastics, resorting to an awkwardly-worded sentence in order to prove one's thesis, although all other evidence point to a completely different and an only logical conclusion. And I'd also like to say that despite the Prosecution's claim, it is not true that the document bears the stamp of the military police. The document bears the stamp of the 3rd Battalion of the Military Police, precisely the unit to which the document was sent. Your Honours, even the Prosecutor, in paragraph 293 of their final brief, claims that the military police often reported about infringements and crimes committed by Tuta's units. We claim that on the case file there's a series of documents which show that police investigations were undertaken against those people and that criminal reports were filed. Due to the time restrictions, we're not in a position to cite all of them. Therefore, we are pointing to just a few of them: P6727, P6893, 5D4168, 5D4169, 5D5022. In paragraphs 1046 through 1055 of their final brief, in the part that concerns Valentin Coric, the Prosecutor claims that Coric commanded the military police as well as supported the military police engagement in combat, although he knew only too well that that would have a negative impact on the policing, especially in crime prevention and fight against crime. However, quite contrary to that thesis, the Prosecution, in the same final brief in paragraphs 565 and 752, which concern the accused Stojic and Praljak, asserts that Coric tried to intervene quite legitimately in order to withdraw the military police from the front-line in order for them to be able to fight crime. In paragraph 742 and 748 of their final brief, the Prosecution admitted that General Praljak was the one who obstructed Coric's request and that General Praljak was the one who kept the military police on the front-lines. Your Honours, this is yet another example how the Prosecutor uses the same facts and interprets them in different ways, depending on the goal that they wish to achieve. The Defence asserts that Valentin Coric, within the limitations of his powers and abilities, did everything that he possibly could to actively fight crime of all types. And just like the Prosecution asserts in paragraphs 565 and 752, this is why he sent the request for the military police to be withdrawn from the front-lines in order to be able to do their normal policing. This is recorded in Exhibit P5471. The Prosecutor's expert Tomljanovic confirmed that the military police had manpower issues and that these issues reflected negatively on their crime/combat capabilities, especially in 1993, when military policemen were engaged in combat. This was recorded on transcript pages 6347 and 6348. Moreover, in their final brief, the Prosecutor claims that the Prosecutor Witness Biskic had a different position than Coric with regard to the engagement of military police in combat, implying that the witness did not agree with Coric's actions, and that Biskic was actually the one who finally withdrew the military police from the front-lines once Coric had left the position. Contrary to the allegations by the Prosecution, in his testimony before this Trial Chamber, Witness Biskic didn't criticise Coric. Actually, he absolutely supported his position, and he totally agreed with the intentions and positions that arise from document P5471, and that was recorded on transcript pages 15279 and the following. Contrary to the Prosecutor's allegations, Biskic actually testified that he wasn't the one who was in a position to withdraw the military police from the front-lines. Actually, it was done by General Praljak's successor, at his request. That was General Roso, who was also the new chief of the Main Staff in December 1993. This was recorded on transcript page 15282. Therefore, again in this case the Prosecutor maintains a position contrary to the positions of his own witnesses, one of whom is an expert witness. He erroneously interprets the testimonies of their own witnesses. He ignores parts of testimony which doesn't support his thesis, and all that with an objective to confirm their construct at all costs, although that construct is not founded in any of the evidence on file. The testimony of Biskic was corroborated by Defence Witness Vidovic. He said that behind document P5471 was a sincere desire for the military police to withdraw from the battle-field in order to be able to fight crime, and that was recorded on transcript page 51518. Defence Witness, 1D, the late Mr. Buntic confirmed that the issue of the military police engagement in combat was discussed at HVO sessions, and that was recorded on transcript pages 30566 and the following. Once all the evidence is reviewed, it's very difficult to understand how the Prosecutor, based on document P5471, which is Valentin Coric's request for the military police to be withdrawn from the front-lines, can draw a conclusion that that corroborates a criminal behaviour. Your Honour, Coric's intentions presented in that request were honourable and sincere, which is corroborated by the fact that he, in his capacity as the minister of the interior, already in November 1993, immediately after having taken up the position, sent another one, an almost identical request. However, at that time the request concerned the civil police. Proof of that is document P6837. The only possible and logical and viable conclusion which can be drawn from this action of my client is that that was a benevolent and appropriate step in the fight against crime. Your Honours, I am about to embark on a somewhat lengthier and bigger topic. So since I only have five minutes left, I would like to conclude today and resume tomorrow.

I believe that you have another two and a half hours, but Madam Registrar is going to give me the exact time. Tomorrow, we resume at 2.15, and on Thursday we're supposed to sit in the morning at 9.00. So tomorrow, we shall continue with the Coric Defence arguments, and after that we will hear from Pusic's Defence. And I would like to wish everybody a good evening. Until tomorrow.
